For the principal value put t=x^q, then split at one and substitute t=1/u on the upper piece.

Using the transform of an infinite exponential tail

pedagogy.difficultyRationale: A recursively defined density is recognized as convolution before its transform is taken, avoiding expansion of a growing piecewise polynomial. Solve-time and difficulty estimates are editorial, not measured player calibration.

solutionSteps: \text{Induction in the recursion shows that the functions are nonnegative and supported on their indicated intervals.}

analyticCertificate: The modulus of sum_{j=0}^{n-1} exp(ijx) is |sin(nx/2)/sin(x/2)|.
Its squared modulus has Fourier coefficient n-|k| for |k|<n.
Parseval gives 2pi(n^2+2 sum_{k=1}^{n-1}(n-k)^2)=2pi n(2n^2+1)/3.
At multiples of 2pi the quotient is extended continuously; there is no singularity.
assumptions: Integer n>=2; continuous endpoint extension of the quotient.

choices.misconception: correct
Using the second moment instead of fourth
Counting ordered pairs without their frequency constraint
Including the forbidden endpoint frequency in the autocorrelation

pedagogy.difficultyRationale: A fourth power of an oscillatory quotient becomes an additive-pair count through autocorrelation and Parseval, rather than repeated trigonometric expansion. Solve-time and difficulty estimates are editorial, not measured player calibration.

solutionSteps: \text{Squaring and integrating leaves only pairs of opposite frequencies.}

analyticCertificate: Each pole has nonzero positive residue parameter and the poles are distinct. One-sided endpoint limits and the displayed positive derivative give a bijection on each pole interval. P_y has degree s+1 and cannot vanish at a pole; its s+1 real simple roots are precisely those branches. Vieta plus the inverse function theorem proves the Jacobian sum. The nonnegative transformed integrand is integrable, so monotone convergence on bounded y-intervals justifies the entire improper identity. Near a pole the displayed integrand tends to zero as a positive even power; at infinity it decays as x^(-2m). The cosine-power recurrence follows by integration by parts with vanishing endpoint terms; its base case is the interval length pi.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{Keep all inverse branches of the displayed rational map. Write its poles and positive weights in the following general form.}

\textnormal{On every interval between successive poles, including the two unbounded intervals, the map increases from negative infinity to positive infinity. Thus each real y has exactly s plus one simple real preimages.}
\textnormal{No pole is a zero of this polynomial. Its roots are exactly the preimages. The coefficient of its second-highest power gives their sum.}
\textnormal{The inverse function theorem gives positive inverse derivatives. Differentiating the finite root sum makes their sum exactly one.}

\textnormal{The branch substitutions are valid first on bounded image intervals; nonnegativity permits the improper limit. A tangent substitution reduces the remaining integral to the standard cosine-power recurrence.}

Multiplication by the finite sine polynomial sin(t)cos(t)^j permits orthogonality term by term by L2 convergence, not an unjustified pointwise boundary interchange. The finitely many roots cos(k*pi/(n+1)),1<=k<=n, are simple and interior. The nonnegative defect |p|-p*sigma has zero integral only if it vanishes almost everywhere; continuity on each sign interval then forces the required alternating signs. pedagogy.difficultyRationale: A sign function annihilating all lower-degree polynomials proves the global L1 optimum; equality forces every sign-change root and gives the unique minimizer.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{Use a polynomial whose sign is orthogonal to every polynomial of smaller degree. Define the second-kind Chebyshev polynomials by their recurrence.}
U_0(x)=1,\quad U_1(x)=2x,\quad U_{j+1}(x)=2xU_j(x)-U_{j-1}(x),\quad U_j(\cos t)=\frac{\sin((j+1)t)}{\sin t}.

\textnormal{The leading coefficient of U is two to its degree, so q is monic. Under x equal to cosine t, every lower-degree monomial times the Jacobian is a finite linear combination of sine modes of frequency at most n.}

\textnormal{Indeed, the square-wave sign has only odd multiples of frequency n plus one in its sine expansion; sine orthogonality eliminates every lower frequency. Equivalently, integrating separately on its finitely many sign intervals gives the same identities.}
\textnormal{The difference between any monic p and q has degree below n. The sign moment identities therefore give a universal lower bound.}

\textnormal{Equality requires p to have the sign of U almost everywhere. At every simple interior zero of U its sign changes, so continuity forces a zero of p there. There are n such distinct roots; monicity forces p to equal q.}
\textnormal{The displayed next-to-leading coefficient follows by substituting the leading two coefficients into the recurrence.}

solutionSteps: \textnormal{The phase is nonnegative and vanishes only at the interior point zero and the endpoint one. Their orders determine different localization scales.}

\textnormal{Near zero put x equal to n to the power minus one over two p times u. Near one put one minus x equal to n to the power minus one over two q times v. The logarithmic tilt is asymptotically constant on each rescaled neighborhood.}
n^{\tau x}=\exp(\tau x\ln n),\qquad n^{-1/(2p)}\ln n\to0,\quad n^{-1/(2q)}\ln n\to0.
\textnormal{Let J zero and J one denote the masses in fixed small neighborhoods of zero and one, respectively.}
\textnormal{Away from both neighborhoods the phase has a positive minimum, so the exponential decay defeats every fixed power from the tilt.}

\textnormal{For the local dominated limits, the phase bounds give an exponential of a negative even power. The residual tilted linear term has a coefficient tending to zero, and can be absorbed into half that negative power plus a fixed constant. This supplies an integrable bound.}
\textnormal{The factor x in the numerator tends to zero at the first well and one at the second. It is bounded, so the same domination justifies those weighted limits.}
\textnormal{The two powers match. The limiting first moment is the endpoint mass divided by the sum of both local masses.}

\textnormal{Interchange the continuous triangular integral and collect the quadrature evaluations. The resulting kernel is piecewise quadratic.}
\textnormal{The kernel is negative near both endpoints and positive in the middle. Its two interior zeros determine the exact absolute integral.}

\textnormal{Choose continuous second derivatives bounded by one that agree with the kernel sign outside shrinking neighborhoods of the two zeros. Integrating them twice gives admissible functions; dominated convergence makes their errors tend to this bound.}

\textnormal{Equality would require the second derivative to equal the kernel sign almost everywhere, up to one common sign. Continuity would then force opposite one-sided values at each sign-changing zero. This is impossible, so the supremum is not attained.}

\textnormal{Interchange the continuous triangular integral and collect the quadrature evaluations. The resulting kernel is piecewise quadratic.}
\textnormal{The kernel is negative near both endpoints and positive in the middle. Its two interior zeros determine the exact absolute integral.}

\textnormal{Choose continuous second derivatives bounded by one that agree with the kernel sign outside shrinking neighborhoods of the two zeros. Integrating them twice gives admissible functions; dominated convergence makes their errors tend to this bound.}

\textnormal{Equality would require the second derivative to equal the kernel sign almost everywhere, up to one common sign. Continuity would then force opposite one-sided values at each sign-changing zero. This is impossible, so the supremum is not attained.}

pedagogy.difficultyRationale: The mean constraint interacts with a nonconvex two-well cost: a supporting envelope gives the infimum, while continuous recovery sequences and incompatible endpoint values decide attainment.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{The nonconvex cost has two zero wells. The best lower bound must allow mixtures of those wells rather than apply Jensen directly to the quartic.}
\textnormal{Nonnegativity gives a lower bound of zero. A measurable mixture with the prescribed mean takes the two well values in the following proportions.}

\textnormal{For a strictly mixed mean, put the single interior transition at t zero as follows. Use linear ramps from minus two to minus one on the first interval, from minus one to one across the middle interval, and from one to two on the last interval. On the remaining intervals keep the neighboring well value.}

\textnormal{Attaining zero cost would force the continuous function to take only the two well values everywhere. It could not have either of the prescribed endpoint values; by continuity an endpoint neighborhood already has positive cost.}
\textnormal{Thus the lower bound is an infimum reached by a sequence, and is not attained by any admissible continuous function.}

solutionSteps: \textnormal{Compare the entire class with the increasing trajectory generated by the reciprocal growth integral. Define the growth function and its increasing integral.}
\textnormal{For an arbitrary admissible u, its accumulated right side is a differentiable majorant v. Monotonicity of the growth function gives an upper differential inequality for v.}
\textnormal{Before the limiting value of G, invert this inequality. It gives one finite bound for every member of the class.}
T<T_*\quad\Longrightarrow\quad u(t)\le v(t)\le G^{-1}(T)\quad(0\le t\le T).
\textnormal{To test the critical endpoint, fix any positive N and follow the exact increasing trajectory until it reaches N. Then keep it constant. Define that finite continuous function as follows.}
t_N=G(N)<T_*,\qquad u_N(t)=\begin{cases}G^{-1}(t),&0\le t\le t_N,\\N,&t_N\le t\le T.\end{cases}

\textnormal{Up to the joining time it satisfies equality in the integral equation. Afterwards the right side keeps increasing, while the function stays at N. Thus it remains an admissible subsolution.}

\textnormal{If T reaches or exceeds the critical time, all such truncated trajectories fit in the interval. Their heights are unbounded as N increases, so no common finite bound exists. Evaluate the critical integral by a tangent substitution and the cosine-power recurrence.}

J(f)\le C_p\int_{\mathbb R}g(u)^2\,\mathrm du,\qquad C_p=\int_{\mathbb R}k_p(t)\,\mathrm dt.
\textnormal{With the exponential substitution, the kernel mass is an Euler beta integral. Both endpoints converge because the shape parameter is positive.}
\textnormal{To prove this constant cannot be lowered, use normalized indicators of longer and longer intervals in logarithmic coordinates.}
\textnormal{Dominated convergence applies with the integrable kernel as majorant. These are admissible nonzero functions for every positive L, so the bound is sharp.}
\textnormal{Finally, equality would make every translation defect vanish for almost every shift. The following nonnegative identity makes the obstruction explicit.}
C_p\int_{\mathbb R}g^2-J(f)=\frac12\int_{\mathbb R}k_p(t)\int_{\mathbb R}(g(u)-g(u-t))^2\,\mathrm du\,\mathrm dt.

\textnormal{Translations are continuous in the L2 norm. Since the kernel is strictly positive, equality forces translation invariance for every shift. A translation-invariant L2 function on the real line is constant almost everywhere, and the only such square-integrable constant is zero. This contradicts the required nonzero squared integral.}
